value: harbour seals respond to a variety of different vortex rings upon vibrissal stimulation
method: operant detection: seals trained to indicate the side on which a hydrodynamic stimulus (single vortex ring from an acrylic vortex ring generator, 30 cm from the aperture of the blend to the bite target) was perceived; 10 rings (S1 to S10) differing in size, velocities, acceleration and duration; visually opaque mask, headphones with pink noise
conditions: two experimentally naive male harbour seals (Filou, Moe) in captivity; unilateral (ipsilateral vibrissal array) stimulation in the detection experiment; all ten rings were detected with highly significant performance (chi-square, P<0.001, N=45 per ring, Fig. 4 caption); when a nylon stocking mask covered the vibrissae both seals dropped to chance (Moe 50%, Filou 36.67% correct, chi-square P>0.05, N=30); a pressure-wave control (latex sheet over the apertures) gave 55.33% (Moe) and 56.67% (Filou) correct over rings S1 to S7, P>0.05, N=150 each, five sessions; chance 50% (side choice); the same paper's minimum hydrodynamically perceivable angle (5.7 deg, not reached) and travel-direction results are not filed here; water temperature not reported in the text read

units: cm/s (maximum water velocity within the artificial breathing current; one value per seal)
method: blindfolded seals searched a platform 1 m below the surface for the one of eight nozzles emitting an artificial flatfish breathing current (nozzles at 45 deg); flow fields quantified with particle image velocimetry; threshold = flow velocity at 29% performance (7 of 24 trials, significant at the 5% level) read from a quadratic fit of performance against velocity
conditions: two male harbour seals, Henry (19 years) and Luca (13 years), tested in a netted enclosure in a netted enclosure separated from the sea by a net; free swimming over the platform; 24 trials per session, 13 sessions per seal at five stimulus velocities (7.4 down to 2.6 cm/s); the two values are two individuals, not an uncertainty range (Henry 4.2, Luca 3.7 cm/s, from the Results); average background noise 2.9 cm/s (Henry) and 2.5 cm/s (Luca), measured daily after the sessions, so it may have been higher during trials; vibrissal mediation not tested by covering the whiskers in this paper; no headphones mentioned; water temperature not reported in the text read; signal-to-noise ratios at threshold 1.4 (Henry) and 1.5 (Luca); background 2.4 to 3.4 cm/s in Henry's sessions and 1.8 to 3.4 in Luca's, so both thresholds lie just above measured background

value: 90% of trials ended in successful trail-following (444 of 495)
method: a second seal was trained to search for and follow the hydrodynamic trail left by a trail-generating seal in a kidney-shaped pool, once the generator had left the water; trail structure measured with particle image velocimetry; trial successful when the seal followed the trail to one of nine end points or came within one body length (1.5 m) of it; chance level for this criterion P = 0.14
conditions: one test seal (Nick, 3-year-old male, the trained animal of Dehnhardt et al. 2001) following the trail of one generator seal (Malte, 3-year-old naive male), both captive-born; opaque elastic mask over the eyes with the vibrissae uncovered and headphones with pink noise during the search; 495 trials over nine courses, performance never below 80% on any course; in 278 of the 444 successful trials (63%) the seal followed the trail and hardly ever diverged from it; with the vibrissae covered the same seal did not succeed, but it refused to start searching at all (number of control trials not reported); water temperature not reported in the text read

value: all three seals performed significantly better than chance finding the active nozzle, blindfolded and non-blindfolded
method: platform 1 m below the surface with eight nozzles (2 to 3 cm beneath a grid, 135 cm crosswise and 110 cm lengthwise apart) emitting an artificial flatfish breathing current (maximal flow velocities 20 to 25 cm/s, 1 to 3 cm extension at vibrissa level); seals trained to search for the active opening and station there for 5 s; chance 0.125 (one in eight), cumulative binomial test
conditions: three male harbour seals, Luca (12 years), Filou (8 years), Henry (18 years), kept in a netting enclosure in the Marina Hohe Duene, Rostock, on the Baltic Sea; constant-current trials: Filou and Luca 54 trials per nozzle, 27 of them blindfolded (Henry 560 trials, split not stated); detection highly significant for all three animals in both conditions (P much less than 0.1%); pulsed-current trials used two seals (Luca, Henry) and were also significant; water temperature not reported and headphones not mentioned in the text read; behavioural controls covered eyes and vibrissae with a stocking mask (two trials per nozzle per animal, over two sessions, mixed with non-blindfolded trials; no count or statistic reported): the seals found no active nozzle and mostly drifted at the surface refusing to search, so the control does not separate loss of the sense from refusal; no headphones; hydrophone and stethoscope checks found no acoustic difference between active and inactive nozzles; background flow 0.5 to 7.2 cm/s and only Luca's performance correlated with it (P = 0.025)

value: 93.7% correct moving direction at a 5 s delay
method: two-alternative (left/right) forced choice: a fin-like paddle moved through calm water in an experimental box, and after a set delay the seal indicated the direction of the paddle's movement from the remaining hydrodynamic trail; Bernoulli test against chance
conditions: one 6-year-old male harbour seal (Henry); opaque stocking mask with the vibrissae uncovered and headphones with pink noise; fin 2 mm thick, 227 mm2, moved at about 0.2 m/s at 0.8 m depth; 20 sessions of up to 30 trials (pseudorandom delay and direction), of which 180 trials were filmed; chance 50% (left/right); delays 5, 10, 20, 25, 30 and 35 s analysed, performance above chance for 5 to 35 s (P<0.01 for 5 to 30 s, P=0.012 at 35 s) and not above chance for delays of 40 s and longer; the paper reports 91.3% and 87.5% at 10 and 20 s, 73.8%, 75% and 70.6% at 25, 30 and 35 s; training criterion at least 90% correct in three consecutive sessions; trials per delay and water temperature not given in the text read; with the vibrissae covered by a nylon stocking the seal could not find the gate and failed the procedure (no count given)
